Returns:
    `True` if the launch mode is supported by the platform; otherwise `False`.

methods.name: supports_close_for_launch_mode
methods.doc:
Checks whether `close_in_app_web_view` is supported for a launch mode.

Args:
    mode: Launch mode to verify close support for.

Returns:
    `True` if closing an in-app web view is supported; otherwise `False`.

classes.name: OpenUrl
classes.doc:
Opens a URL when the control is activated.

Equivalent to :meth:`flet.UrlLauncher.launch_url`, but performed by the
client inside the user's gesture, so that opening a new tab is not blocked as
an unsolicited popup.

Example:
    ```python
    ft.Button(
        "Open flet.dev",
        action=ft.OpenUrl("https://flet.dev", target=ft.UrlTarget.BLANK),
    )
    ```

fields.name: url
fields.doc: The URL to open.

fields.name: target
fields.doc:
Where to open the URL, for example :attr:`flet.UrlTarget.BLANK` for a new tab.

    Web-only; ignored on other platforms.

classes.name: UserAccelerometerReadingEvent
classes.doc: Like :class:`~flet.AccelerometerReadingEvent`, this is a discrete reading from an     accelerometer and measures the velocity of the device. However, unlike     :class:`~flet.AccelerometerReadingEvent`, this event does not include the effects     of     gravity.

fields.name: x
fields.doc: Linear acceleration along the X axis, gravity removed, in `m/s^2`.

fields.name: y
fields.doc: Linear acceleration along the Y axis, gravity removed, in `m/s^2`.

fields.name: z
fields.doc: Linear acceleration along the Z axis, gravity removed, in `m/s^2`.

fields.name: timestamp
fields.doc: Event timestamp.

classes.name: UserAccelerometer
classes.doc:
Streams linear acceleration readings.

If the device is still, or is moving along a straight line at constant speed,
the reported acceleration is zero. If the device is moving e.g. towards north
and its speed is increasing, the reported acceleration is towards north;
if it is slowing down, the reported acceleration is towards south;
if it is turning right, the reported acceleration is towards east.
The data of this stream is obtained by filtering out the effect of gravity
from :class:`~flet.AccelerometerReadingEvent`.

Note:
    * Supported platforms: Android, iOS and web.
    * Web ignores requested sampling intervals.

fields.name: enabled
fields.doc: Whether the sensor should be sampled. Disable to stop streaming.

fields.name: interval
fields.doc:
Desired sampling interval provided as a :class:`~flet.Duration`.
    Defaults to 200 ms.

fields.name: cancel_on_error
fields.doc: Whether the stream subscription should cancel on the first sensor error.

fields.name: on_reading
fields.doc:
Fires when a new reading is available.

    `event` contains `x`, `y`, `z` acceleration values and `timestamp`
    (microseconds since epoch).

fields.name: on_error
fields.doc: Fired when the platform reports a sensor error. `event.message` is the error     description.

classes.name: Wakelock

classes.name: TemplateRoute
classes.doc:
Matches a concrete route string against parameterized route templates.

Instances keep the original route in `route` and expose matched template
parameters as dynamic attributes after a successful call to `match()`.
Parameter attributes captured by a previous match are reset to `None` before
each new matching attempt, preventing stale values from leaking between
checks.

Only the path of the route is matched; a query string and a `#` fragment are
ignored, so `/books/42?tab=reviews` matches `/books/:id` with `id` set to
`"42"`. Read query string parameters with :attr:`flet.Page.query`.

members.name: FADE

members.name: VISIBLE

members.name: IDEOGRAPHIC

classes.name: TextThemeStyle
classes.doc:
Predefined Material text style roles from the active theme.

Use these values with properties such as :attr:`flet.Text.theme_style`
to reference semantic typography slots (display, headline, title, body, label)
instead of hard-coding font metrics in each control.

members.name: DISPLAY_LARGE
members.doc:
Largest display style.

    Intended for very prominent, short text on large surfaces, such as hero headlines.

members.name: DISPLAY_MEDIUM
members.doc:
Medium display style.

    Intended for high-impact short text when :attr:`DISPLAY_LARGE` is too dominant.

members.name: DISPLAY_SMALL
members.doc:
Smallest display style.

    Intended for concise, emphasized text that still needs display-level prominence.

members.name: HEADLINE_LARGE
members.doc:
Largest headline style.

    Headline styles are below display styles and suit short, high-emphasis headings.

members.name: HEADLINE_MEDIUM
members.doc:
Medium headline style.

    Suitable for section headers and prominent in-content headings.

members.name: HEADLINE_SMALL
members.doc:
Smallest headline style.

    Suitable for compact headline usage on dense layouts.

members.name: TITLE_LARGE
members.doc:
Largest title style.

    Titles are typically used for medium-emphasis, short text such as card titles.

members.name: TITLE_MEDIUM
members.doc:
Medium title style.

    Suitable for secondary titles and emphasized labels in structured content.

members.name: TITLE_SMALL
members.doc:
Smallest title style.

    Suitable for compact title text where space is limited.

members.name: LABEL_LARGE
members.doc:
Largest label style.

    Commonly used for component text, such as button labels and prominent captions.

members.name: LABEL_MEDIUM
members.doc:
Medium label style.

    Suitable for compact UI labels in controls and supporting interface text.

members.name: LABEL_SMALL
members.doc:
Smallest label style.

    Suitable for dense, low-footprint labels and small supporting annotations.

members.name: BODY_LARGE
members.doc:
Largest body style.

    Body styles are intended for longer passages and primary reading content.

members.name: BODY_MEDIUM
members.doc:
Medium body style.

    Common default style for standard paragraph text in Material-themed UIs.

members.name: BODY_SMALL
members.doc:
Smallest body style.

    Suitable for secondary body text, footnotes, and compact long-form content.

classes.name: TextStyle
classes.doc: A style describing how to format and paint text.

fields.name: size
fields.doc:
The size of glyphs (in logical pixels) to use when painting the text.

    Defaults to `14`.

fields.name: height
fields.doc:
The height of this text span, as a multiple of the font size.

    See detailed explanation
    [here](https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/painting/TextStyle/height.html).

fields.name: weight
fields.doc:
The typeface thickness to use when painting the text (e.g., bold).

    Defaults to :attr:`flet.FontWeight.NORMAL`.

fields.name: italic
fields.doc: Whether to use italic typeface.

fields.name: decoration
fields.doc: The decorations to paint near the text (e.g., an underline).

fields.name: decoration_color
fields.doc: The color in which to paint the text decorations.

fields.name: decoration_thickness
fields.doc: The thickness of the decoration stroke as a multiplier of the thickness defined by     the font.

fields.name: decoration_style
fields.doc:
The style in which to paint the text decorations (e.g., dashed).

    Defaults to `TextDecorationStyle.SOLID`.

fields.name: font_family
fields.doc: See https://flet.dev/docs/controls/text#font_family.

fields.name: font_family_fallback
fields.doc:
Ordered fallback font families to use when glyphs are not available in
    :attr:`font_family`.

fields.name: color
fields.doc: Text foreground https://flet.dev/docs/types/colors.

fields.name: bgcolor
fields.doc: Text background https://flet.dev/docs/types/colors.

fields.name: shadow
fields.doc:
A list of shadows painted underneath the text.

    Multiple shadows can be used to simulate lighting from multiple sources. Shadow
    order matters because different orders can produce different transparency results.

fields.name: foreground
fields.doc: The paint drawn as a foreground for the text.

fields.name: letter_spacing
fields.doc: The amount of space (in logical pixels) to add between each letter. A negative     value can be used to bring the letters closer.

fields.name: word_spacing
fields.doc: The amount of space (in logical pixels) to add at each sequence of white-space     (i.e. between each word). A negative value can be used to bring the words closer.

fields.name: overflow
fields.doc: How visual text overflow should be handled.

fields.name: baseline
fields.doc: The common baseline that should be aligned between this text span and its parent     text span, or, for the root text spans, with the line box.

classes.name: StrutStyle
classes.doc:
Defines the strut used for vertical text layout.

A strut sets the minimum line height relative to the baseline and applies to every
line in the paragraph. It is useful when text may vary in script or font metrics
but should still keep a predictable vertical rhythm.

fields.name: size
fields.doc:
The size of text (in logical pixels) to use when getting metrics from the font.

    Defaults to `14`.

fields.name: height
fields.doc:
The minimum height of the strut, as a multiple of :attr:`size`.

    See detailed explanation here:
    https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/painting/StrutStyle/height.html

fields.name: weight
fields.doc:
The typeface thickness to use when calculating the strut.

    Defaults to :attr:`flet.FontWeight.W_400`.

fields.name: italic
fields.doc: Whether to use italic typeface.

fields.name: font_family
fields.doc: See :attr:`flet.Text.font_family`.

fields.name: leading
fields.doc:
The amount of additional space to place between lines when rendering text.

    Defaults to using the font-specified leading value.

fields.name: force_strut_height
fields.doc:
Whether the strut height should be forced.

    Defaults to `False`.

classes.name: PageTransitionTheme
classes.doc:
Page transition preset for route changes.

These could, for example, be used together with     :class:`~flet.PageTransitionsTheme` to

members.name: NONE

members.name: FADE_UPWARDS
members.doc:
Fade-and-slide transition where the incoming page moves upward,

members.name: OPEN_UPWARDS

Upward reveal transition with clipping/scrim,
    matching the transition used on Android P.

members.name: ZOOM

Zoom/fade transition used by modern Material route animations,
    similar to the one provided in Android Q.

members.name: CUPERTINO

Cupertino-style horizontal page transition,
    which matches native iOS page transitions.

members.name: PREDICTIVE

members.name: FADE_FORWARDS

Assigned to :attr:`flet.Theme.page_transitions` to
override how Material routes animate on each target platform.

Transition preset for Android routes.

    If `None`, defaults to :attr:`flet.PageTransitionTheme.FADE_UPWARDS`.

fields.name: ios

Transition preset for iOS routes.

    If `None`, defaults to :attr:`flet.PageTransitionTheme.CUPERTINO`.

fields.name: linux
fields.doc:
Transition preset for Linux desktop routes.

    If `None`, defaults to :attr:`flet.PageTransitionTheme.ZOOM`.

fields.name: macos
fields.doc:
Transition preset for macOS desktop routes.

    If `None`, defaults to :attr:`flet.PageTransitionTheme.ZOOM`.

fields.name: windows
fields.doc:
Transition preset for Windows desktop routes.

    If `None`, defaults to :attr:`flet.PageTransitionTheme.ZOOM`.

classes.name: ColorScheme
classes.doc:
A set of more than 40 colors based on the [Material     spec](https://m3.material.io/styles/color/the-color-system/color-roles) that can     be used to configure the color properties of most components.
Read more about color schemes in
[here](https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/material/ColorScheme-class.html).

fields.name: primary
fields.doc: The color displayed most frequently across your app's screens and components.

fields.name: on_primary
fields.doc: A color that's clearly legible when drawn on :attr:`primary`.

fields.name: primary_container
fields.doc: A color used for elements needing less emphasis than :attr:`primary`.

fields.name: on_primary_container
fields.doc: A color that's clearly legible when drawn on :attr:`primary_container`.

fields.name: secondary
fields.doc: An accent color used for less prominent components in the UI, such as filter     :class:`~flet.Chip`s, while expanding the opportunity for color expression.

fields.name: on_secondary
fields.doc: A color that's clearly legible when drawn on :attr:`secondary`.

fields.name: secondary_container
fields.doc: A color used for elements needing less emphasis than :attr:`secondary`.

fields.name: on_secondary_container
fields.doc: A color that's clearly legible when drawn on :attr:`secondary_container`.

fields.name: tertiary
fields.doc: A color used as a contrasting accent that can balance :attr:`primary` and     :attr:`secondary` colors or bring heightened attention to an element, such as an     input field.

fields.name: on_tertiary
fields.doc: A color that's clearly legible when drawn on :attr:`tertiary`.

fields.name: tertiary_container
fields.doc: A color used for elements needing less emphasis than :attr:`tertiary`.

fields.name: on_tertiary_container
fields.doc: A color that's clearly legible when drawn on :attr:`tertiary_container`.

fields.name: error
fields.doc: The color to use for input validation errors, e.g. for     :attr:`flet.FormFieldControl.error`.

fields.name: on_error
fields.doc: A color that's clearly legible when drawn on :attr:`error`.

fields.name: error_container
fields.doc: A color used for error elements needing less emphasis than :attr:`error`.

fields.name: on_error_container
fields.doc: A color that's clearly legible when drawn on :attr:`error_container`.

fields.name: surface
fields.doc: The background color for widgets like :class:`~flet.Card`.

fields.name: on_surface
fields.doc: A color that's clearly legible when drawn on :attr:`surface`.

fields.name: on_surface_variant
fields.doc: A color that's clearly legible when drawn on :attr:`surface_container_highest`.

fields.name: outline
fields.doc: A utility color that creates boundaries and emphasis to improve usability.

fields.name: outline_variant
fields.doc: A utility color that creates boundaries for decorative elements when a 3:1     contrast isn’t required, such as for dividers or decorative elements.

fields.name: shadow
fields.doc: A color use to paint the drop shadows of elevated components.

fields.name: scrim

fields.name: on_tertiary_fixed_variant

fields.name: secondary_fixed

fields.name: tertiary_fixed

classes.name: TextTheme
classes.doc:
Customizes :class:`~flet.Text` styles.

Material 3 design
[defines](http://localhost:3000/docs/controls/text#pre-defined-theme-text-styles)
5 groups of text styles with 3 sizes in each group: "Display", "Headline", "Title",
"Label" and "Body" which are used across Flet controls.

fields.name: body_large
fields.doc: Largest of the body styles. Body styles are used for longer passages of text.

fields.name: body_medium
fields.doc:
Middle size of the body styles. Body styles are used for longer passages of text.
    The default text style for Material.

fields.name: body_small
fields.doc: Smallest of the body styles.

fields.name: display_large
fields.doc: Largest of the display styles. As the largest text on the screen, display styles     are reserved for short, important text or numerals. They work best on large     screens.

fields.name: display_medium
fields.doc: Middle size of the display styles.

fields.name: display_small
fields.doc: Smallest of the display styles.

fields.name: headline_large
fields.doc:
Largest of the headline styles. Headline styles are smaller than display styles.
    They're best-suited for short, high-emphasis text on smaller screens.

fields.name: headline_medium
fields.doc: Middle size of the headline styles.

fields.name: headline_small
fields.doc: Smallest of the headline styles.

fields.name: label_large
fields.doc: Largest of the label styles. Label styles are smaller, utilitarian styles, used     for areas of the UI such as text inside of components or very small supporting     text in the content body, like captions. Used for text on :class:`~flet.Button`,     :class:`~flet.TextButton` and :class:`~flet.OutlinedButton`.

fields.name: label_medium
fields.doc: Middle size of the label styles.

fields.name: label_small
fields.doc: Smallest of the label styles.

fields.name: title_large
fields.doc: Largest of the title styles. Titles are smaller than headline styles and should be     used for shorter, medium-emphasis text.

fields.name: title_medium
fields.doc: Middle size of the title styles.

fields.name: title_small
fields.doc: Smallest of the title styles.

classes.name: ScrollbarTheme
classes.doc: Customizes the colors, thickness, and shape of descendant scrollbars.

fields.name: thumb_visibility
fields.doc: Indicates that the scrollbar thumb should be visible, even when a scroll is not     underway. When `False`, the scrollbar will be shown during scrolling and will fade     out otherwise. When `True`, the scrollbar will always be visible and never fade     out. Property value could be either a single boolean value or a dictionary with     `ft.ControlState` as keys and boolean as values.

fields.name: thickness
fields.doc: The thickness of the scrollbar in the cross axis of the scrollable. Property value     could be either a single float value or a dictionary with `ft.ControlState` as     keys and float as values.

fields.name: track_visibility
fields.doc: Indicates that the scrollbar track should be visible. When `True`, the scrollbar     track will always be visible so long as the thumb is visible. If the scrollbar     thumb is not visible, the track will not be visible either. Defaults to `False`     when `None`. If this property is `None`, then `ScrollbarTheme.track_visibility` of     `Theme.scrollbar_theme` is used. If that is also `None`, the default value is     `False`. Property value could be either a single boolean value or a dictionary     with `ft.ControlState` as keys and boolean as values.

fields.name: radius
fields.doc: The Radius of the scrollbar thumb's rounded rectangle corners.

fields.name: thumb_color
fields.doc: Overrides the default Color of the Scrollbar thumb. The value is either a single     color string or `ft.ControlState` dictionary.

fields.name: track_color
fields.doc: Overrides the default Color of the Scrollbar track. The value is either a single     color string or `ft.ControlState` dictionary.

fields.name: track_border_color
fields.doc: Overrides the default Color of the Scrollbar track border. The value is either a     single color string or `ft.ControlState` dictionary.

fields.name: cross_axis_margin
fields.doc:
Distance from the scrollbar thumb to the nearest cross axis edge in logical     pixels.
    The scrollbar track consumes this space. Must not be null and defaults to 0.

fields.name: main_axis_margin
fields.doc: Distance from the scrollbar thumb's start and end to the edge of the viewport in     logical pixels. It affects the amount of available paint area. The scrollbar track     consumes this space. Mustn't be null and defaults to 0.

fields.name: min_thumb_length
fields.doc: The preferred smallest size the scrollbar thumb can shrink to when the total     scrollable extent is large, the current visible viewport is small, and the     viewport is not overscrolled.

fields.name: interactive
fields.doc: Whether the Scrollbar should be interactive and respond to dragging on the thumb,     or tapping in the track area. When `False`, the scrollbar will not respond to     gesture or hover events, and will allow to click through it. Defaults to `True`     when `None`, unless on Android, which will default to `False` when `None`.

classes.name: InputDecorationTheme
classes.doc:
Customizes the decoration of descendant :class:`~flet.TextField` and
:class:`~flet.Dropdown` controls: their border, label, hint and helper
styles, padding and fill.

A control's own properties win over the theme. A control with no
:attr:`~flet.FormFieldControl.border` uses the theme's :attr:`border`.

Example:
    A soft resting border that darkens on hover and turns to the primary
    color on focus:

    ```python
    page.theme = ft.Theme(
        input_decoration_theme=ft.InputDecorationTheme(
            border=ft.OutlineInputBorder(
                border_radius=8,
                side=ft.BorderSide(
                    color=ft.Colors.with_opacity(0.24, ft.Colors.ON_SURFACE)
                ),
            ),
            label_style=ft.TextStyle(size=14),
            hint_style=ft.TextStyle(size=14),
        ),
    )
    ```

fields.name: border
fields.doc:
The border drawn around the decorated input area, for every state.

    Accepts a single :class:`~flet.InputBorder` or a dictionary mapping
    :class:`~flet.ControlState`s to :class:`~flet.InputBorder`s. Supported
    state keys are :attr:`~flet.ControlState.DEFAULT`,
    :attr:`~flet.ControlState.HOVERED`, :attr:`~flet.ControlState.FOCUSED`,
    :attr:`~flet.ControlState.ERROR` and :attr:`~flet.ControlState.DISABLED`.

    The `DEFAULT` entry (or the single border) sets the shape for all states
    and the line for the resting state only. Each other state uses the `side`
    of its own entry if given, otherwise the Material default for that state -
    so setting only a soft resting color keeps the darker hover line and the
    primary-colored, thicker focus line.

classes.name: ThemeSurfaces
classes.doc:
How surface colors of a :class:`~flet.Theme` are derived from its
:attr:`~flet.Theme.color_scheme_seed`.

members.name: NEUTRAL
members.doc:
Surfaces use a neutral grey ramp with no hue: white in light mode and
    near-black (`#121212`) in dark mode. Accent colors (primary, secondary,
    tertiary and their containers) still come from the seed.

    The full list of neutral colors is in the
    [Theming](https://flet.dev/docs/cookbook/theming#surfaces) guide.

members.name: TONAL
members.doc:
Surfaces are tinted with the seed hue, as in the Material 3 default
    color scheme. This was the default before Flet 1.1.0.

classes.name: Theme
classes.doc: Customizes the overall appearance of the application.

fields.name: color_scheme_seed
fields.doc:
Overrides the default color scheme seed used to generate
    :class:`~flet.ColorScheme`.
    The default color is blue.

    The seed drives accent colors. Surfaces are neutral unless
    :attr:`surfaces` is set to :attr:`~flet.ThemeSurfaces.TONAL`.

fields.name: surfaces
fields.doc:

classes.name: WebRenderer
classes.doc:
Selects which Flutter web renderer should be used for a web-hosted app.

Use this with the `web_renderer` argument of :func:`flet.run` or
:func:`flet.run_async`.

Note:
    The available renderer choices depend on how the web frontend was built.
    A default web build provides CanvasKit. A WebAssembly build can make both
    CanvasKit and skwasm available.

members.name: AUTO
members.doc:
Lets the runtime choose the renderer automatically.

    In WebAssembly builds, Chromium-based browsers prefer skwasm and other
    browsers fall back to CanvasKit; in default web builds, CanvasKit is used.

members.name: CANVAS_KIT
members.doc:
Uses the CanvasKit renderer.

    CanvasKit is broadly compatible with modern browsers and is the default
    renderer for web builds. Compared to skwasm, it is significantly faster
    at exchanging byte buffers between JavaScript and Dart, which Flet apps
    do on every UI update.

members.name: SKWASM
members.doc:
Uses the skwasm renderer.

    skwasm is available for WebAssembly web builds and can provide better
    rendering performance, at the cost of slower byte-buffer exchange across
    the JavaScript/Dart boundary. Browsers and servers must meet the
    requirements for WebAssembly support, and multi-threaded rendering
    additionally requires the necessary SharedArrayBuffer security setup.

classes.name: RouteUrlStrategy
classes.doc:
Controls how routes are represented in the browser URL for web apps.

Use this with the `route_url_strategy` argument of :func:`flet.run` or
:func:`flet.run_async`.

Note:
    This setting affects web-hosted apps only.

members.name: PATH
members.doc:
Stores routes in the browser pathname.

    URLs look like `https://example.com/store`.

    Note:
        This strategy usually requires the web server to rewrite unmatched requests to
        `index.html` so deep links and page reloads continue to work.

members.name: HASH
members.doc:
Stores routes in the URL fragment after `#`.

    URLs look like `https://example.com/#/store`.

    This strategy is useful when you cannot configure the hosting server for
    pathname-based routing.

classes.name: NotchShape
classes.doc:
A shape with a notch in its outline.

Typically used as the outline of a 'host' control to make a notch that
accommodates a 'guest' control.
e.g the :class:`~flet.BottomAppBar` may have a notch to accommodate
the :class:`~flet.FloatingActionButton`.

This class is not intended to be used directly. See usable derivatives:

- :class:`~flet.AutomaticNotchShape`
- :class:`~flet.CircularRectangleNotchShape`

classes.name: CircularRectangleNotchShape
classes.doc: A rectangle with a smooth circular notch.

fields.name: inverted
fields.doc: Whether the notch should be placed at the bottom of the rectangle.

classes.name: AutomaticNotchShape
classes.doc:
A notch shape created from :class:`~flet.ShapeBorder` values.

It uses one shape as the outer outline and optionally subtracts a second shape
to form the notch. This is commonly used for controls such as
:class:`~flet.BottomAppBar` that need to make room for a floating action button.

fields.name: host
fields.doc:
The shape of the control that uses the notch.

    This is typically the outer shape of the host control, such as a
    :class:`~flet.BottomAppBar`.

    Note:
        The shape must not depend on text direction.

fields.name: guest
fields.doc:
The shape to subtract from :attr:`host` to create the notch.

    This is typically the shape of the control the notch should accommodate, such as
    a :class:`~flet.FloatingActionButton`.

    If this is `None`, no notch is cut out even when space for a guest control is
    available.

    Note:
        The shape must not depend on text direction.

classes.name: BlendMode
classes.doc:
Algorithms used to combine source and destination pixels during painting.

The source is the content being drawn and the destination is the content already
present behind it.

members.name: CLEAR
members.doc: Drops both the source and destination, leaving a fully transparent result.

members.name: COLOR
members.doc:
Takes the hue and saturation from the source and the luminosity from the
    destination.

members.name: COLOR_BURN
members.doc:
Darkens the destination by dividing the inverse destination by the source and
    then inverting the result.

members.name: COLOR_DODGE
members.doc: Brightens the destination by dividing it by the inverse of the source.

members.name: DARKEN
members.doc: Chooses the darker value from each source and destination color channel.

members.name: DIFFERENCE
members.doc:
Subtracts the smaller channel value from the larger one.

    Compositing black has no effect, while compositing white inverts the other image.

members.name: DST
members.doc: Drops the source and keeps only the destination.

members.name: DST_A_TOP
members.doc: Draws the destination over the source, but only where they overlap.

members.name: DST_IN
members.doc:
Keeps the destination only where the source and destination overlap.

    The source acts as an opacity mask.

members.name: DST_OUT
members.doc:
Keeps the destination only where the source and destination do not overlap.

    The source acts as an opacity mask.

members.name: DST_OVER
members.doc: Draws the source underneath the destination.

members.name: EXCLUSION
members.doc: Produces an effect similar to :attr:`DIFFERENCE`, but softer.

members.name: HARD_LIGHT
members.doc: Combines multiply and screen-style blending while favoring the source image.

members.name: HUE
members.doc:
Takes the hue from the source and the saturation and luminosity from the
    destination.

members.name: LIGHTEN
members.doc: Chooses the lighter value from each source and destination color channel.

members.name: LUMINOSITY
members.doc:
Takes the luminosity from the source and the hue and saturation from the
    destination.

members.name: MODULATE
members.doc: Multiplies the source and destination color channels without multiplying alpha.

members.name: MULTIPLY
members.doc: Multiplies the source and destination color channels, including alpha.

members.name: OVERLAY
members.doc: Combines multiply and screen-style blending while favoring the destination image.

members.name: PLUS
members.doc:
Adds the source and destination channel values together.

    This is useful for cross-fading between two images.

members.name: SATURATION
members.doc:
Takes the saturation from the source and the hue and luminosity from the
    destination.

members.name: SCREEN
members.doc:
Multiplies the inverted source and destination values, then inverts the result.

    This can only produce the same or lighter colors.

members.name: SOFT_LIGHT
members.doc: Applies a softer lighting effect than :attr:`OVERLAY`.

members.name: SRC
members.doc: Drops the destination and keeps only the source.

members.name: SRC_A_TOP
members.doc: Draws the source over the destination, but only where they overlap.

members.name: SRC_IN
members.doc:
Keeps the source only where the source and destination overlap.

    The destination acts as an opacity mask.

members.name: SRC_OUT
members.doc:
Keeps the source only where the source and destination do not overlap.

    The destination acts as an opacity mask.

members.name: SRC_OVER
members.doc:
Draws the source over the destination.

    This is the default painting behavior.

members.name: VALUES
members.doc:
Not a usable blend mode.

    Warning:
        This member exists in the Python enum surface but does not map to a runtime
        blend mode. Do not use it for painting or image composition.

members.name: XOR
members.doc: Uses an exclusive-or composition so overlapping areas become transparent.

classes.name: ScrollMode
classes.doc:
Defines scrolling behavior and scroll bar visibility for scrollable controls.

When assigned to :attr:`flet.ScrollableControl.scroll`, for example, each value
internally maps to a specific :class:`~flet.Scrollbar` configuration.

members.name: AUTO
members.doc:
Scrolling is enabled and scroll bar is only shown when scrolling occurs.

    :class:`~flet.Scrollbar` equivalent:

    ```python
    ft.Scrollbar(
        thickness=4.0 if page.platform.is_mobile() and not page.web else None,
    )
    ```

members.name: ADAPTIVE
members.doc:
Scrolling is enabled and scroll bar is always shown when running app as web or     desktop.

    :class:`~flet.Scrollbar` equivalent:

    ```python
    ft.Scrollbar(
        thumb_visibility=page.web or not page.platform.is_mobile(),
        thickness=4.0 if page.platform.is_mobile() and not page.web else None,
    )
    ```

members.name: ALWAYS
members.doc:
Scrolling is enabled and scroll bar is always shown.

    :class:`~flet.Scrollbar` equivalent:

    ```python
    ft.Scrollbar(
        thumb_visibility=True,
        thickness=4.0 if page.platform.is_mobile() and not page.web else None,
    )
    ```

members.name: HIDDEN
members.doc:
Scrolling is enabled, but scroll bar is always hidden.

    :class:`~flet.Scrollbar` equivalent:

    ```python
    ft.Scrollbar(
        thickness=0,
    )
    ```

classes.name: ClipBehavior
classes.doc:
Different ways to clip content.

See [Clip](https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/dart-ui/Clip.html)
from Flutter documentation for ClipBehavior examples.

members.name: NONE
members.doc:
No clip at all.

    This is the default option for most widgets: if the content does not overflow the
    widget boundary, don't pay any performance cost for clipping.

members.name: ANTI_ALIAS
members.doc:
Clip with anti-aliasing.

    This mode has anti-aliased clipping edges, which reduces jagged edges when the clip
    shape itself has edges that are diagonal, curved, or otherwise not axis-aligned.

members.name: ANTI_ALIAS_WITH_SAVE_LAYER
members.doc: Clip with anti-aliasing and saveLayer immediately following the clip.

members.name: HARD_EDGE
members.doc:
Clip, but do not apply anti-aliasing.

    This mode enables clipping, but curves and non-axis-aligned straight lines will be
    jagged as no effort is made to anti-alias.

classes.name: ImageRepeat
classes.doc: How to paint any portions of a box not covered by an image.

members.name: NO_REPEAT
members.doc: Leave uncovered portions of the box transparent.

classes.name: AppLifecycleState
classes.doc: States that an application can be in once it is running.

members.name: SHOW
members.doc:
The application is shown.

    On mobile platforms, this is usually just before the application replaces another
    application in the foreground.

    On desktop platforms, this is just before the application is shown after being
    minimized or otherwise made to show at least one view of the application.

    On the web, this is just before a window (or tab) is shown.

members.name: RESUME
members.doc: The application gains input focus. Indicates that the application is entering a     state where it is visible, active, and accepting user input.

members.name: HIDE
members.doc:
The application is hidden.

    On mobile platforms, this is usually just before the application is replaced by
    another application in the foreground.

    On desktop platforms, this is just before the application is hidden by being
    minimized or otherwise hiding all views of the application.

    On the web, this is just before a window (or tab) is hidden.

members.name: INACTIVE
members.doc:
The application loses input focus.

    On mobile platforms, this can be during a phone call or when a system dialog is
    visible.

    On desktop platforms, this is when all views in an application have lost input
    focus but at least one view of the application is still visible.

    On the web, this is when the window (or tab) has lost input focus.

members.name: PAUSE
members.doc:
The application is paused.

    On mobile platforms, this happens right before the application is replaced by
    another application.

    On desktop platforms and the web, this function is not called.

members.name: DETACH
members.doc:
The application has exited, and detached all host views from the engine.

    This callback is only called on iOS and Android.

members.name: RESTART
members.doc:
The application is resumed after being paused.

    On mobile platforms, this happens just before this application takes over as the
    active application.

    On desktop platforms and the web, this function is not called.

classes.name: MouseCursor
classes.doc: Various mouse cursor types that represent different operations or states.

members.name: ALIAS
members.doc: A cursor indicating that the current operation will create an alias of, or a     shortcut of the item. Typically the shape of an arrow with a shortcut icon at the     corner.

members.name: ALL_SCROLL
members.doc: A cursor indicating scrolling in any direction. Typically the shape of a dot     surrounded by 4 arrows.

members.name: BASIC
members.doc: The platform-dependent basic cursor. Typically the shape of an arrow.

members.name: CELL
members.doc: A cursor indicating selectable table cells. Typically the shape of a hollow plus     sign.

members.name: CLICK
members.doc:
A cursor that emphasizes an element being clickable, such as a hyperlink.
    Typically the shape of a pointing hand.

members.name: CONTEXT_MENU
members.doc: A cursor indicating somewhere the user can trigger a context menu. Typically the     shape of an arrow with a small menu at the corner.

members.name: COPY
members.doc: A cursor indicating that the current operation will copy the item. Typically the     shape of an arrow with a boxed plus sign at the corner.

members.name: DISAPPEARING
members.doc: A cursor indicating that the current operation will result in the disappearance of     the item. Typically the shape of an arrow with a cloud of smoke at the corner.

members.name: FORBIDDEN
members.doc:
A cursor indicating an operation that will not be carried out.
    Typically the shape of a circle with a diagonal line.

members.name: GRAB
members.doc: A cursor indicating something that can be dragged. Typically the shape of an open     hand.

members.name: GRABBING
members.doc: A cursor indicating something that is being dragged. Typically the shape of a     closed hand.

members.name: HELP
members.doc: A cursor indicating help information. Typically the shape of a question mark, or     an arrow therewith.

members.name: MOVE
members.doc: A cursor indicating moving something. Typically the shape of four-way arrow.

members.name: NO_DROP
members.doc:
A cursor indicating somewhere that the current item may not be dropped.
    Typically the shape of a hand with a forbidden sign at the corner.

members.name: NONE
members.doc: Hide the cursor.

members.name: PRECISE
members.doc:
A cursor indicating precise selection, such as selecting a pixel in a bitmap.
    Typically the shape of a crosshair.

members.name: PROGRESS
members.doc: A cursor indicating the status that the program is busy but can still be     interacted with. Typically the shape of an arrow with an hourglass or a watch at     the corner.

members.name: RESIZE_COLUMN
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing a column, or an item horizontally. Typically the     shape of arrows pointing left and right with a vertical bar separating them.

members.name: RESIZE_DOWN
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing an object from its bottom edge. Typically the shape     of an arrow pointing down.

members.name: RESIZE_DOWN_LEFT
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing an object from its bottom-left corner. Typically the     shape of an arrow pointing lower left.

members.name: RESIZE_DOWN_RIGHT
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing an object from its bottom-right corner. Typically the     shape of an arrow pointing lower right.

members.name: RESIZE_LEFT
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing an object from its left edge. Typically the shape of     an arrow pointing left.

members.name: RESIZE_LEFT_RIGHT
members.doc:
A cursor indicating resizing an object bidirectionally from its left or right     edge.
    Typically the shape of a bidirectional arrow pointing left and right.

members.name: RESIZE_RIGHT
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing an object from its right edge. Typically the shape of     an arrow pointing right.

members.name: RESIZE_ROW
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing a row, or an item vertically. Typically the shape of     arrows pointing up and down with a horizontal bar separating them.

members.name: RESIZE_UP
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing an object from its top edge. Typically the shape of     an arrow pointing up.

members.name: RESIZE_UP_DOWN
members.doc:
A cursor indicating resizing an object bidirectionally from its top or bottom     edge.
    Typically the shape of a bidirectional arrow pointing up and down.

members.name: RESIZE_UP_LEFT
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing an object from its top-left corner. Typically the     shape of an arrow pointing upper left.

members.name: RESIZE_UP_LEFT_DOWN_RIGHT
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing an object bidirectionally from its top left or bottom     right corner. Typically the shape of a bidirectional arrow pointing upper left and     lower right.

members.name: RESIZE_UP_RIGHT
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing an object from its top-right corner. Typically the     shape of an arrow pointing upper right.

members.name: RESIZE_UP_RIGHT_DOWN_LEFT
members.doc: A cursor indicating resizing an object bidirectionally from its top right or     bottom left corner. Typically the shape of a bidirectional arrow pointing upper     right and lower left.

members.name: TEXT
members.doc: A cursor indicating selectable text. Typically the shape of a capital I.

members.name: VERTICAL_TEXT
members.doc: A cursor indicating selectable vertical text. Typically the shape of a capital I     rotated to be horizontal.

members.name: WAIT
members.doc:
A cursor indicating the status that the program is busy and therefore can not be     interacted with. Typically the shape of an hourglass or a watch.

    This cursor is not available as a system cursor on macOS. Although macOS displays a
    "spinning ball" cursor when busy, it's handled by the OS and not exposed for
    applications to choose.

members.name: ZOOM_IN
members.doc: A cursor indicating zooming in. Typically a magnifying glass with a plus sign.

members.name: ZOOM_OUT
members.doc: A cursor indicating zooming out. Typically a magnifying glass with a minus sign.

classes.name: VisualDensity
classes.doc: Defines the visual density of user interface components.

members.name: STANDARD
members.doc:
The default/standard profile for visual density.

    This default value represents a visual density that is less dense than
    either :attr:`COMFORTABLE` or :attr:`COMPACT`, and corresponds to
    density values of zero in both axes.

members.name: COMPACT
members.doc:
The profile for a "compact" interpretation of visual density.

    Individual components will interpret the density value independently, making
    themselves more visually dense than :attr:`STANDARD` and :attr:`COMFORTABLE` to
    different degrees based on the Material Design specification of the
    :attr:`COMFORTABLE` setting for their particular use case.

    It corresponds to a density value of `-2` in both axes.

members.name: COMFORTABLE
members.doc:
The profile for a "comfortable" interpretation of visual density.

    Individual
    components will interpret the density value independently, making themselves more
    visually dense than :attr:`STANDARD` and less dense than :attr:`COMPACT`
    to different degrees based on the Material Design specification of the
    comfortable setting for their particular use case.

    It corresponds to a density value of `-1` in both axes.

members.name: ADAPTIVE_PLATFORM_DENSITY
members.doc:
Visual density that is adaptive based on the given platform.

    For desktop platforms, this returns :attr:`COMPACT`, and for other platforms,
    it returns a default-constructed visual density.

classes.name: Locale
classes.doc: An identifier used to select a user's language and formatting preferences.

fields.name: language_code
fields.doc:
The primary language subtag/code of the locale, e.g `en` for English.

    Its value is case-sensitive and must be a registered subtag in the
    [IANA Language Subtag Registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/language-subtag-registry/language-subtag-registry)
    with the type "language". If you use a deprecated subtag, it will be internally
    modified to its “Preferred-Value”, if it has one. For example: `Locale("he")`
    and `Locale("iw")` are equal, and both have the `language_code="he”`,
    because `iw` is a deprecated language subtag which has been replaced by `he`.

    When there is no language subtag, this parameter should be set
    to `"und"` (the default), which represents an undefined language code.

fields.name: country_code
fields.doc:
The country code or region subtag of the locale, e.g `US` for the United States.

    Its value is case-sensitive and must be a registered subtag in the
    [IANA Language Subtag Registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/language-subtag-registry/language-subtag-registry)
    with the type "region". If you use a deprecated subtag, it will be internally
    modified to its “Preferred-Value”, if it has one. For example: `Locale("de", "DE")`
    and `Locale("de", "DD")` are equal, and both have the `country_code="DE”`,
    because `DD` is a deprecated region subtag which has been replaced by `DE`.

    Locales may also be defined without this, to specify a generic fallback for a
    particular script.

fields.name: script_code
fields.doc:
The script code/subtag of the locale, e.g. `Hant` for Traditional Chinese or     `Hans` for Simplified Chinese. It is especially recommended to set this property     explicitly for languages with more than one script.

    Its value must be a valid Unicode Language Identifier script subtag as listed in
    [Unicode CLDR supplemental
    data](https://github.com/unicode-org/cldr/blob/master/common/validity/script.xml).

classes.name: LocaleConfiguration
classes.doc: Represents the configuration for supported locales and the current locale.

fields.name: supported_locales
fields.doc:
A list of locales that the application supports for localization.

    Note:
        - Locales unsupported/invalid are ignored.
        - Order matters: Locale resolution is performed by progressively relaxing
            specificity until a match is found. Matching is attempted in the following
            priority order:

            1. language + script + country
            2. language + script
            3. language + country
            4. language only
            5. country only (only if no language-based match is found)

            When multiple supported locales match at the same priority level,
            the first matching locale in `supported_locales` is selected.
            If no supported locale matches at any level, the first entry in
            `supported_locales` is used as the final fallback.
        - For languages with multiple scripts or regional variants, include locales in
            increasing order of specificity: language-only → language+script →
            language+script+country. Defining all of these variants is not strictly
            required, but doing so greatly improves locale resolution and reduces
            ambiguous matches. Omitting intermediate fallbacks can lead to incorrect
            script or regional selection in edge cases—for example, a Simplified
            Chinese user in Taiwan (`zh_Hans_TW`) may incorrectly resolve to
            Traditional Chinese if `zh_Hans` and `zh_Hans_CN` are not present.

    Example: Full Chinese support for CN (Mainland China), TW (Taiwan), and HK (Hong
    Kong)
        ```python
        supported_locales = [
            # Generic Chinese (fallback for all Chinese variants)
            Locale(language_code="zh"),

            # Script-level variants
            Locale(language_code="zh", script_code="Hans"), # Simplified Chinese zh_Hans
            Locale(language_code="zh", script_code="Hant"), # Traditional Chinese
            zh_Hant

            # Region-specific variants
            Locale(language_code="zh", script_code="Hans", country_code="CN"), #
            zh_Hans_CN
            Locale(language_code="zh", script_code="Hant", country_code="TW"), #
            zh_Hant_TW
            Locale(language_code="zh", script_code="Hant", country_code="HK"), #
            zh_Hant_HK
        ]
        ```

fields.name: current_locale
fields.doc:
The current locale.

    Note:
        - Must be an item of :attr:`supported_locales` to take effect.
        - If `None` or invalid/unsupported, the first supported locale in
            :attr:`supported_locales` is used.

classes.name: SupportsStr
classes.doc: Structural protocol for objects that provide a string representation.

classes.name: Prop
classes.doc:
Descriptor for sparse property tracking on `BaseControl` and `Value`
types.

Each public, non-skip field gets replaced by a `Prop` instance by
`_install_props()`.  The descriptor stores only *non-default* values in
`obj._values`, so the frozen diff fast-path only needs to examine the
union of keys from two objects' `_values` dicts rather than scanning
every declared field.

classes.name: Value
classes.doc:
Marker class for non-control value types that have sparse `_values`
tracking enabled via `@value`.

`@value` handles all setup — you never need to inherit from this
class explicitly.  It is exposed so that `isinstance(obj, Value)`
checks work in the diff machinery.
